summary: Pyrazinamide is a first-line antitubercular agent used during the initial 2 months of a 6-month (or longer) regimen for drug-susceptible active tuberculosis, always combined with other effective agents such as isoniazid and rifampin. It is dosed by weight (15-30 mg/kg once daily). Major risks are dose-related hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia, which may precipitate acute gout. It is contraindicated in severe hepatic damage, hypersensitivity, and acute gout.
indications: Initial treatment of active tuberculosis in adults and children, combined with other antituberculous agents (CDC: isoniazid + rifampin + pyrazinamide for 2 months, then isoniazid + rifampin for 4 months in drug-susceptible disease)
Treatment after failure with other primary drugs in any form of active tuberculosis
Component of individualized regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis

moa: Pyrazinamide is a pyrazine analogue of nicotinamide. Its mechanism of action is not fully known. It is active only at slightly acidic pH, conditions found within phagolysosomes of macrophages and in caseous tuberculous lesions, where it is bacteriostatic or bactericidal against M. tuberculosis depending on the concentration achieved. It is hydrolyzed in the liver to its active metabolite pyrazinoic acid, which is believed to mediate its antimycobacterial effect, allowing it to sterilize semidormant organisms and shorten overall TB therapy.

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is not known whether pyrazinamide can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. Give to a pregnant woman only if clearly needed.
lact: Pyrazinamide has been found in small amounts in breast milk. Use with caution in nursing mothers, weighing the risk-benefit of therapy.
renal: Approximately 70% of a dose is excreted renally, mainly by glomerular filtration. Patients with impaired renal function do not appear to require a dose reduction, though it may be prudent to use the low end of the dosing range. The plasma half-life may be prolonged in renal impairment. Pyrazinamide is dialyzable.
hepatic: Contraindicated in severe hepatic damage. Hepatotoxicity is the principal serious adverse effect and is dose-related; it may occur at any time during therapy. Obtain baseline liver function and uric acid, follow high-risk patients closely, and discontinue (and do not resume) if signs of hepatocellular damage appear. The half-life may be prolonged in hepatic impairment.

pearls: Never use as monotherapy - always part of a multidrug TB regimen, typically the first 2 months
Hepatotoxicity is dose-related and can occur at any time; baseline and periodic LFTs are essential
Hyperuricemia is common and usually asymptomatic; discontinue if accompanied by acute gouty arthritis
Most active at acidic pH, making it effective against intracellular/semidormant organisms and key to shortening therapy

missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered with the rest of the TB regimen; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume the schedule. Do not double up. Stress adherence - missed doses promote treatment failure and resistance.
overdose: Overdose experience is limited; one case report described reversible abnormal liver function tests that normalized after stopping the drug. Use clinical monitoring and supportive therapy; pyrazinamide is dialyzable.
